rationale: Human diet studies used ungraded olive oil and aggregate symptom scores. The 2026 cohort analyzed a whole-diet score. Cold-pressed oil and postural instability remain unresolved.

The green-tea genetic proxy showed a nominal opposite association with baseline hyposmia that failed multiplicity correction. A separate habitual-intake comparison found no clear difference in binary hyposmia. Neither measured severity change after brewed tea.
The cassia study evaluated inhaled fragrance and sleep quality. Ground cinnamon consumption and daytime sleepiness were outside the comparison.

A blinded Parkinson trial reported lower depression scores with oral tablets containing whole ground saffron. A separate capsule trial also reported a favorable depression signal. Tablet and capsule regimens limit generalization to culinary use.
The local walnut oil study tested a cultured-cell model. It contains no human Parkinson symptom outcome.

The extra-virgin oil trial excluded neurological causes and compared two active oils. The Parkinson trials tested a broader Mediterranean pattern and found no clear between-group constipation benefit.
The Lithuanian cohort recorded ungraded olive oil use and modeled an overall dietary score. It did not estimate an extra-virgin olive oil effect on urinary urgency.
The black-tea association was with a composite motor score in LRRK2-related Parkinson's. Brewing details and a separate bradykinesia effect remain unresolved.
The Parkinson diet survey recorded cumin intake and anxiety measures. It did not isolate toasted cumin or a specific anxiety effect.
The chocolate crossover measured a composite motor endpoint. The synbiotic and chocolate study used rats. Neither study measured anxiety change after plain dark chocolate in people with Parkinson's.
Human data on unspecified coconut oil used overall symptom scores. The preclinical study used virgin oil. Refined oil and postural instability remain unresolved.
The cassia study used aromatherapy. It did not test fatigue after consuming ground cinnamon.
A survey recorded coffee or caffeine as a fatigue coping strategy without measuring change after brewed coffee. A caffeine-capsule trial did not establish a fatigue effect for this preparation.
The brewed green tea pilot measured broader clinical scales. It did not isolate handwriting size.
A Parkinson survey recorded lemon balm use and pooled perceived effects. It did not estimate a depression effect for the frozen preparation.
A human Parkinson trial used sesame oil in both arms as a carrier. It could not isolate toasted oil or its effect on pain.
The virgin coconut oil paper used cells and rats. The human dietary trial used an MCT supplement as part of a broader diet. Neither established a virgin coconut oil effect on dyskinesia.
A small mixed-diagnosis constipation study used a multi-herb extract that included a Zanthoxylum ingredient. It could not isolate toasted Sichuan pepper.
The marjoram pilot used filtered tea and measured a composite motor score. Fresh marjoram and postural instability were outside that comparison.
The saffron powder tablet trial reported an overall sleep-quality score. It did not report a separate effect on insomnia severity.
Parkinson trials used formulated curcumin and did not isolate swallowing difficulty after grated turmeric.
The virgin coconut oil study used cells and an animal model. It did not measure fatigue in people with Parkinson's.
The marjoram study tested tea and aggregate motor scores. It did not estimate walking slowness after consuming dried leaves.
The Parkinson cassia trial used inhaled fragrance. The dietary survey did not isolate ground cinnamon or establish its effect on anxiety.
The spice study used pepper as an odor stimulus. It did not measure an effect of consuming ground black pepper on olfactory impairment.
The black-tea cohort result concerned a composite motor score in LRRK2-related Parkinson's. It did not isolate a brewed-tea effect on walking slowness.
Participants with more advanced Parkinson's consumed less cold potato salad in a standardized meal study. It did not test whether boiled potatoes alter swallowing difficulty.
The Lithuanian cohort modeled whole-diet adherence and recorded ungraded oil use. It did not isolate cold-pressed olive oil or an anxiety effect.
Caraway served as an odor stimulus in the Parkinson study. It did not test the effect of consuming toasted caraway.
The relevant Parkinson studies used formulated curcumin and composite scores. They did not isolate a rigidity effect of grated turmeric.
A rat study evaluated rotarod and locomotor outcomes. A human study used sesame oil in both trial arms. Neither estimates fall frequency after toasted sesame oil in Parkinson's.
Curcumin studies tested supplements and aggregate outcomes. They did not measure freezing episodes after ground turmeric.
The saffron trial reported a global cognition score for ground powder tablets. Dried saffron and executive function were outside the tested contrast.
In a hemodialysis trial, constipation improved over time in all three oil groups. The trial did not study cold-pressed flaxseed oil in people with Parkinson's.
The saffron study reported a fatigue improvement after ground saffron tablets. The frozen claim specifies dried saffron as consumed.
Curcumin trials used formulated supplements and clinical scores at study visits. They did not estimate the effect of ground turmeric on daily off-time duration.
The Parkinson studies used nanomicelle or phospholipid curcumin. A bradykinesia-specific effect of ground turmeric remains unresolved.
The virgin coconut oil study had no human Parkinson participants or clinical sleepiness measure.
The Parkinson spice study measured identification of cardamom odor. It did not test an effect of consuming ground cardamom.
Dairy cohort results concern diagnosis risk. They do not measure change in facial expressiveness after pasteurized cow's milk.
The dietary cohort used ungraded olive oil and a whole-diet score. An extra-virgin oil effect on rest tremor was not isolated.
The Ginger-PD registration has no posted result. The older constipation study tested a mixed herbal extract and cannot isolate grated ginger.
Dietary studies used ungraded olive oil and composite or whole-diet comparisons. Cold-pressed oil and a separate bradykinesia endpoint were unresolved.
The Parkinson curcumin studies did not test grated turmeric or isolate a walking-speed effect.
The spice study tested mint as an odor stimulus. It did not test a brewed spearmint effect on olfactory impairment.
The dark chocolate crossover measured composite motor scores. It did not assess a specific voice-volume effect.
The dark chocolate crossover measured composite motor scores. It did not establish a speech-intelligibility effect.
Two small crossover studies found no clear Parkinson swallowing-timing benefit after capsaicin extract or a wafer. Ground cayenne consumption and swallowing severity were outside the comparisons.
The flaxseed-derived omega-3 trial also administered vitamin E and measured total UPDRS. It cannot isolate cold-pressed flaxseed oil or rest tremor.
The Parkinson diet survey did not isolate ground cinnamon. Its composite nonmotor results do not establish a constipation effect.
Dairy cohorts measured the probability of Parkinson's diagnosis. They did not measure speech intelligibility after pasteurized cow's milk.
The marjoram pilot tested tea and composite nonmotor and depression scores. Dried leaves as consumed and insomnia severity were outside the tested contrast.
The sage finding was about recognizing an odor stimulus. It did not test effects of ground sage consumption.
The curcumin supplement studies did not isolate pain severity after ground turmeric in Parkinson's.
The nanomicelle curcumin trial measured overall sleep quality. It did not report a separate daytime-sleepiness effect or test grated turmeric.
Marjoram was an odor stimulus in the identification study. Separate tea studies did not test an olfactory effect of consuming dried leaves.
The virgin coconut oil paper used preclinical models. Human data on unspecified oil were cross-sectional and did not isolate dream enactment.
The Parkinson constipation trial compared dietary patterns. It did not estimate an independent effect of boiled pinto beans.
The flaxseed-derived omega-3 trial combined the supplement with vitamin E and used total UPDRS. It did not estimate muscle rigidity after cold-pressed flaxseed oil.
The black-tea cohort association concerned a composite motor score in LRRK2-related Parkinson's. It did not isolate rest tremor or the brewed preparation.
The flaxseed-derived omega-3 plus vitamin E trial did not isolate cold-pressed flaxseed oil or a bradykinesia outcome.
The brewed-tea pilot measured fatigue in 14 participants. Scores rose, but the uncontrolled and statistically inconclusive change does not establish worsening.
The spice study used cinnamon in odor identification. It did not measure an effect of ground cinnamon ingestion on olfactory impairment.
